prompt: charge(due, back) answered 200, 200 and then 400 with the same two dates. Why?

choices.text: It reads a global that was rebound between the calls
choices.why: Right. daily_fine became 100, and charge depends on it although its signature does not say so.

choices.text: The dates are compared differently on the third call
choices.why: Date arithmetic is deterministic; the arguments were identical every time.

choices.text: Appending to fines_charged doubles the next result
choices.why: The log is written, never read, by charge; it is the global rate that changed.

prompt: Which of these functions are pure? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: fine(due, returned, daily=50), which returns a number of cents
choices.why: Right. Its whole input is in its signature and it changes nothing.

choices.text: A function that returns the loans due before date.today()
choices.why: It reads the clock, so the same call answers differently on another day.

choices.text: notices(loans, today), which appends to a list it created and returns it
choices.why: Right. The list is born inside the call; no caller sees it change.

choices.text: A function that sorts the list it was given in place and returns None
choices.why: The caller still holds that list, so the mutation escapes.

prompt: Being able to replace a call such as fine(due, back) by its value anywhere without changing the program is called ___ transparency.
After renew_in_place(first), the history list shows 30 March as the due date. Why?

choices.text: The history was printed after a second renewal
choices.why: There was one renewal; the history simply holds the same object.

choices.text: Python copies objects into lists and renew_in_place updated the copy too
choices.why: Python never copies on append; it stores a reference, which is the whole bug.

choices.text: The history held a reference to the loan, not a copy
choices.why: Right. Every holder of the object sees the edit, so the record became false.

prompt: Member is a frozen dataclass with titles: list[str]. bia.titles.append("Dom Casmurro") succeeds. What is the fix the section gives?

choices.text: Hold a tuple, so the value is immutable all the way down
choices.why: Right. A frozen object is only as immutable as what it holds; a tuple has no append.

choices.text: Add frozen=True a second time, on the field
choices.why: frozen is a class option; it protects fields from reassignment and nothing deeper.

choices.text: Nothing: frozen dataclasses copy their lists on every access
choices.why: No copy is made; the append changed the one list the member holds.

prompt: What does replace(loan, due=new_date) do to the original loan?

choices.text: Nothing; it returns a new Loan with that field changed
choices.why: Right. The old value is untouched, which is why the history kept 16 March.

choices.text: It edits the due date in place, bypassing frozen
choices.why: It never edits; a frozen instance refuses assignment even from the library.

choices.text: It deep-copies every field, including the title string, into new memory
choices.why: Fields are copied by reference: the new loan shares its title with the old one.

prompt: In core.py and shell.py, where is date.today() allowed to be called?

choices.text: In days_late, where the date is needed
choices.why: That would make the core impure and its tests depend on the calendar.

choices.text: Only in the shell
choices.why: Right. The core takes today as an argument; the shell reads the clock or the command line.

choices.text: In both, as long as the results are the same
choices.why: Reading the clock in the core is the impurity the split exists to remove.

prompt: Put what main() in shell.py does in order.
items: Read the date and load the loans
Call the core to decide the notices
trap: The core sits in the middle: read, decide, write. Nothing is written before the decision exists.

prompt: Lesson 13's remind took a send function; core.notices returns Notice values instead. When does the lesson say injection is still needed?

choices.text: Whenever there are tests, since values cannot be asserted
choices.why: Values are the easiest thing to assert; test_core.py does exactly that.

choices.text: Never; returning values always replaces it
choices.why: Not always: some cores have to act in the middle of their work.

choices.text: When the core must act midway, say read one record depending on another
choices.why: Right. A core whose job ends in a decision can return it; one that needs an effect partway through needs it passed in.

prompt: gentle = pipeline(per_day(50), capped(500)). What is gentle(12), in cents?
hint: pipeline applies the steps left to right.

prompt: Inside per_day, the returned fine still knows cents after per_day has returned. What is that called?

choices.text: A global variable
choices.why: cents is local to one call of per_day; per_day(50) and per_day(100) each keep their own.

choices.text: A frozen dataclass field set when the function was defined
choices.why: No class is involved; functions capture variables by themselves.

choices.text: A closure
choices.why: Right. The inner function captures the variable of the call that made it.

prompt: A FinePolicy interface has one method and no state, with a class per policy. What does the section suggest?

choices.text: Use functions: with one method and no state, the function is the strategy
choices.why: Right. Norvig's point: once functions are values, several patterns shrink to a line.

choices.text: Keep the classes: a strategy must be a class to be a pattern
choices.why: The pattern is the idea of swapping the algorithm; the class is one way to hold it.

choices.text: Merge every policy into one function with an if per policy
choices.why: That brings back the switch lesson 14 removed.

prompt: After reduce consumed fines, list(fines) printed []. Why?

choices.text: map returns an iterator, and reduce had used it up
choices.why: Right. Iterators yield each value once; make a list first if you need it twice.

choices.text: reduce empties any list it is given, to save memory
choices.why: reduce does not modify a list; fines was never a list.

choices.text: filter removed every loan on the second pass
choices.why: There is no second pass: the iterators were already exhausted.

prompt: Match each part of the comprehension sum(days_late(l) * 50 for l in LOANS if days_late(l) > 0) to the job it does.
A developer from TypeScript writes late = filter(...) in Python, then loops over late twice. What happens on the second loop?

choices.text: The same items, as with array.filter in TypeScript
choices.why: That is the TypeScript behaviour; Python's filter is lazy and single-use.

choices.text: A TypeError, because an iterator cannot be looped over twice
choices.why: Nothing is raised; the second loop simply finds nothing, which is worse.

choices.text: No items at all, silently
choices.why: Right. The first loop exhausted the iterator, and an exhausted iterator yields nothing without complaint.

prompt: Why does parse_loan return Err for a bad line instead of raising?

choices.text: Raising exceptions is slower than returning in Python
choices.why: Speed is not the argument; the failure being an expected outcome is.

choices.text: date.fromisoformat cannot raise, so there is no exception to pass on
choices.why: It does raise ValueError for 30 February; parse_loan catches it and turns it into an Err.

choices.text: match statements only work with values, never with exceptions
choices.why: True of match, but the choice of Result came first and for another reason.

choices.text: A bad line is expected, and the import must report every one
choices.why: Right. Returned errors are data; the loop goes on and prints three errors out of five lines.

prompt: The configuration file that names the database is missing at start-up. Following the section's table, what should the code do?

choices.text: Raise, and let the program stop loudly
choices.why: Right. A missing configuration is not something ordinary callers handle; it should crash where someone will see it.

choices.text: Return Err from every function up to main, layer by layer
choices.why: Returning it through every layer is the noise the table warns about.

choices.text: Return an Ok with an empty database name and carry on
choices.why: That hides the failure as a value that lies, the worst of both.

prompt: What does a type checker such as mypy add to the Ok | Err return type?

choices.text: It converts exceptions into Err values automatically
choices.why: A checker changes nothing at run time; parse_loan does the converting.

choices.text: It runs parse_loan on sample lines to find failures
choices.why: mypy reads code, it does not execute it.

choices.text: It refuses .value until the code has checked which case it holds
choices.why: Right. The failure case has to be handled before the code passes the check.

prompt: Match each language to where its immutability stops.

pairs.right: A frozen object holding a list can still have the list changed
final stops reassignment, not mutation of what the field points to
A struct copy still shares the slices and maps inside it
readonly is checked at compile time only

prompt: A Go reviewer asks you to replace a chain of generic Map and Filter helpers with a plain loop. How does the lesson read that?

choices.text: As a gap in your design that the loop will fix
choices.why: The design can be equally functional with a loop; the request is about idiom.

choices.text: As the language's culture: the loop is idiomatic Go
choices.why: Right. Go never adopted map and filter as a style, and pure functions still sit inside the loop.

choices.text: As proof that Go cannot pass functions as values
choices.why: Go has had closures from the start.

prompt: A teammate wraps an impure fine function with functools.cache "for speed". What goes wrong?

choices.text: Nothing; cache works the same on any function
choices.why: It works only if the answer depends on the arguments alone.

choices.text: It returns stale answers when the hidden input changes
choices.why: Right. A cached charge would keep answering 200 after the rate became 100, and log nothing.

choices.text: Python refuses to cache a function that reads a global
choices.why: Python cannot tell; purity is a discipline it does not check.

prompt: A notice batch must be sent at 08:00 from a list of loans held by two threads. Which design keeps this lesson's guarantees?

choices.text: Each thread renews loans in place and the sender reads the shared list
choices.why: Mutation of shared objects is exactly the aliasing problem; the sender may see half a renewal.

choices.text: A notices function that calls date.today() and sends each e-mail as it decides
choices.why: That mixes the clock, the decision and the effect, which the core and shell split apart.

choices.text: Frozen loans, a pure notices(loans, today), and the send in the shell
choices.why: Right. Immutable values are safe to share, the decision is pure, and the one effect sits at the edge.

prompt: pipeline(capped(500), per_day(50)) is applied to 15 days. What does it return, and why?

choices.text: 500, because the cap always wins
choices.why: Order matters: here the cap runs first, on the days.

choices.text: An error, because capped expects cents
choices.why: Both are ints; nothing checks the unit, which is why the order is easy to get wrong.

choices.text: 25000, because the steps run right to left as in mathematics
choices.why: Right to left would cap 750 at 500, not give 25000; and this pipeline runs left to right.

choices.text: 750: the cap meets 15 days, not cents, and lets it through
choices.why: Right. Left to right, min(15, 500) is 15, then 15 * 50 is 750.
